projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: My dear Pound: I have been suffering rather badly from an attack of rheumatism which I have succeeded in keeping out of my eyes so far. Miss Weaver writes that Mr Pinker has not yet drawn up the agreement. I have written to him instructing him to do so at once and to her informing her that if he does not I shall send her a blank signed agreement which he can fill in later at her dictation. As regards terms I have instructed him to accept unconditionally, subject to his commission, whatever terms she is able to propose. She writes that four printing firms have refused to print my novel . One (Messrs Clay and Sons) accepted at first and then refused. She writes also that an ex-clerk of Messrs Maunsel and Co of Dublin who, it seems, is now in the employment of The Egoist informs her that if my book is not published before 1 April (All Fools’ Day) it cannot be published this spring. Possibly he can say also who paid the Irish printer, Falconer, and for £70 to burn the first edition of my book of stories . I confess that I find the re-emergence of this name a bad omen.

Mr Pinker, I presume, is still “doing his best” with the verses and the play I sent him. If a printer is found and time is limited would you read the proofs for me? In return if you like I shall correct the proofs of your next book. If you cannot I suggest that some reader be found and the fee charged to me. In any case I want the book to be published this spring as, until it is out of the way, I cannot continue what I am writing. I had just begun again and now this bad news comes to obstruct me. I am sending this letter express to your address in London to save time. Have you any news from Poetry or from Drama ? I hope that if your article has appeared in the latter review it may be possible for you to print my play when you become editor of your new review. I hope (not only for my sake) that its prospects are still good. I hope also that you are in good health. I wish I could say as much for myself. I could scarcely walk last week but I do not care so long as I do not get a relapse of iritis. Today I feel much better. Perhaps it is due to the stimulus of this bad news.

div.note: JJ and family moved to 19 Kreuzstrasse from 7 Reinhardstrasse, in Zurich, circa 15 October 1915, and remained there until 31 March 1916.
For JJ’s eye trouble and its possible connection with a bout of rheumatic fever, see JJ to Pound, 19 July 1915, notes.

After several publishers declined to publish A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man as a book, JJ, through his London literary agent J.B. Pinker, signed a contract for its issuance with Harriet Shaw Weaver’s Egoist Press in London, which had already published the novel serially in The Egoist. When publication of the book was delayed by the refusal of English printers to set it, B.W. Huebsch of New York published an American edition in December 1916, supplying Weaver with sheets for the first English edition, which the Egoist Ltd. published in February 1917.
For JJ’s instructions to Pinker regarding a contract for A Portrait, see JJ to Pinker, 10 March 1916 (LII 374–75).

Under British law at the time, printers, no less than authors and publishers, could be subject to prosecution for their involvement in the publication of works deemed obscene, libelous, or blasphemous. The prosecution of D.H. Lawrence’s The Rainbow in England in 1915 had made printers and publishers especially cautious. Pound suggested to Weaver and JJ that blank spaces be left for controversial passages in the printed Portrait, and he volunteered to paste typed restorations into copies to form a private edition. The public could then choose between this unexpurgated version and the expurgated one available for ordinary purchase. “And damn the censors,” Pound added (LII 375). A similar strategy of private and public editions was used for Pound’s volume of poems, Lustra, published in England in 1916 and in America in 1917.

Probably Richard Clay and Sons Ltd., London and Bungay, which printed, among other works, Joseph Conrad’s Youth: A Narrative and Two Other Stories (London and Toronto: J.M. Dent & Sons Ltd., 1917), and Henry James’s The American Scene (London: George Bell & Sons, 1907).

JJ had signed a contract in 1909 with Dublin publisher Maunsel & Co. to produce Dubliners. Judging passages in several of the stories to be obscene or libelous, the firm engaged in protracted negotiations with JJ, who refused to alter his text or give a special financial undertaking. After learning of Maunsel’s ultimate decision in 1912 not to publish the book, the Dublin printer John Falconer supposedly destroyed the entire edition of printed sheets (although JJ rescued a single set of proofs). “A Curious History,” Egoist vol. 1, no. 2 (15 January 1914): 26–27, documents the events through a compilation of letters from JJ, with an introduction by Pound.

On 10 February 1916, Pinker wrote JJ that “the verses reached me quite safely, and I am doing my best with them” (John Firth, “James Pinker to James Joyce, 1915–1920,” Studies in Bibliography 21 [1968]: 214). JJ was trying, through Pinker and Pound, to raise some cash by getting some of his poems placed with magazines such as the English Review and The Nation. In early 1916, Pound had submitted two of JJ’s poems to Harriet Monroe, editor of Poetry in Chicago, and JJ sent her others. Five eventually appeared in Poetry, vol. 10, no. 2 (May 1917): 72–75: “Simples,” “Tutto è Sciolto,” “Flood,” “A Flower Given to My Daughter,” and “Nightpiece.” These poems with others were later published as Pomes Penyeach (Paris: Shakespeare and Company, 1927). Also around this time, B.W. Huebsch was trying to become the authorized American publisher of all of JJ’s works, and he wished to publish Chamber Music, originally issued in England in 1907 (LI 91-92). Huebsch’s edition appeared in 1918.

Pinker and Pound were trying to find a producer who would stage Exiles and a publisher who would issue it in a magazine or as a book, without success. Exiles was eventually published in May 1918 by Grant Richards in London and by B.W. Huebsch in New York. It was first performed in a German translation in Munich in 1919.
Pound, burdened with many responsibilities at this time, promptly replied on 16 March 1916: “My proof reading is out of the question. I am incapable, even if I had time” (Pound/Joyce 74).

JJ had begun drafting episodes of Ulysses while in Trieste. In October 1916, he wrote Harriet Shaw Weaver from Zurich: “I have almost finished the first part and have written out part of the middle and end” (LII 387). These sections would become, respectively, the “Telemachia” (episodes 1-3), the “Odyssey” or “Wanderings” (episodes 4-15), and the “Nostos” (episodes 16-18). The letter from June 30, 1915 reports the progress in a different way. (See Michael Groden, Ulysses in Progress [Princeton, NJ: Princeton University Press, 1977], 6.)

Pound’s essay, “Mr. James Joyce and the Modern Stage,” Drama, vol. 6, no. 2 (February 1916): 122–32, discussed Exiles two years before its publication (see JJ to Pound, 19 July 1915, notes). JJ asked Pinker to submit the play itself for publication in Drama, which rejected it later that year. The reference to “your new review” refers to Pound’s proposal to the New York lawyer and patron of the arts, John Quinn (1870-1924), that he fund a literary magazine that Pound would edit. On 27 August 1915, Pound wrote JJ: “[T]here seems a chance of a monthly magazine that can pay contributors. I have spent the day writing a prospectus designed to entrap American dollars” (Pound/Joyce 41). The magazine did not materialize, though Pound began editorial work for The Little Review in 1917, for which Quinn arranged generous financial support.
